# Philip Rubin
Philip Rubin is a distinguished psychologist and linguist known for his interdisciplinary research on embodied cognition, focusing particularly on the biological bases of speech and language. Graduating with a BA from Brandeis University in 1971 and earning a PhD in experimental psychology from the University of Connecticut in 1975, Rubin’s work spans computational modeling, speech synthesis and perception, signal processing, and theoretical approaches to complex temporal events. He developed several pioneering speech synthesis systems, including ASY (articulatory synthesis) and SWS (sinewave synthesis), and contributed to models incorporating gestural computational phonology and task dynamics. Rubin’s leadership roles include directing key research projects at Haskins Laboratories, serving as president of the Auditory-Visual Speech Association, and holding senior positions at the National Science Foundation and the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP), where he led neuroscience initiatives and various science policy efforts.
Beyond his scientific research, Rubin has been active in science policy, advocacy, and ethical oversight related to human subjects research and emerging technologies. He has chaired influential committees on behavioral and cognitive science, testified before Congress, and contributed to the modernization of federal research regulations. Rubin is currently involved in scientific advisory boards and serves as president and chair of the Federation of Associations in Behavioral and Brain Sciences (FABBS). His contributions have been recognized through numerous fellowships and awards, including election to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, the Acoustical Society of America, and the National Academy of Public Administration. Rubin’s career reflects a unique integration of research, policy, ethics, and advocacy in behavioral science and speech technology.
